alt: Penetrating power: alpha particles are stopped by a sheet of paper, beta particles by a few millimetres of aluminium, and gamma rays pass through both and are only reduced in intensity by several centimetres of lead, never stopped completely.
caption: Figure: what stops alpha, beta and gamma radiation

alt: Alpha-particle scattering from gold foil: the relative number detected per unit time falls from 1 000 000 at 10° to 13 000 at 30°, 230 at 90° and 66 at 150°; on a log scale the curve drops steeply then flattens, but a few alpha particles still rebound through large angles.
caption: Figure: alpha particles scattered by a gold foil, number against angle (log scale, values from the lesson table)

alt: Beta energy spectrum: the relative number of beta particles rises to a peak of 100 near 0.10 MeV and falls to zero at the maximum energy of 0.55 MeV, a continuous range, which is why a third particle (the antineutrino) must share the decay energy.
caption: Figure: beta particles have a continuous spread of kinetic energies (values from the lesson table)

alt: Binding energy per nucleon against nucleon number, from the nuclide values in the lesson: 1.11 MeV for deuterium, a local peak of 7.07 MeV for helium-4, rising to a broad maximum of 8.79 MeV at iron-56, then falling slowly to about 7.6 MeV for uranium; fusion of light nuclei and fission of heavy nuclei both move towards the peak and release energy.
caption: Figure: iron-56 is near the peak of the binding-energy curve (lines join the tabulated nuclides)

alt: Boyle's law data: pressure against 1/volume for trapped air at constant temperature gives a straight line through the origin; the six readings from 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa at 30.0 cm³ to 3.01 × 10⁵ Pa at 10.0 cm³ lie on it, and the gradient pV is about 30 × 10⁵ Pa cm³, or 3.0 J.
caption: Figure: p against 1/V is a straight line through the origin, so pV is constant

alt: Charging a capacitor through a resistor: the p.d. and charge rise from zero towards their final values, reaching 63% after one time constant RC, while the current falls from its initial value to 37% in the same time; after 5RC both are within 1% of their limits.
caption: Figure: charging curves share the time constant RC; current decays as p.d. and charge grow

alt: Discharge curve of a 1000 µF capacitor through 47 kΩ from 12 V: the p.d. falls exponentially, V = 12e^(−t/47), to 4.41 V (37%) after one time constant RC = 47 s and 1.62 V (13.5%) after 94 s, never quite reaching zero.
caption: Figure: exponential decay of p.d. in a discharging capacitor, with one time constant marked

alt: Graph of ln V against t for the discharge data: a straight line from an intercept of ln 12 = 2.485 falling by about 0.213 every 10 s, so the gradient is −1/RC = −0.0213 per s and RC = 47 s.
caption: Figure: ln V against t is a straight line whose gradient is −1/RC

alt: Graphs for charging a 2200 µF capacitor from a 12 V battery: the capacitor p.d. rises along a straight line from 0 to 12 V as the charge rises to 26.4 mC; the triangle under it is the energy stored, 158 mJ, and the rectangle under the battery's 12 V line is the energy supplied, 317 mJ, so half is dissipated.
caption: Figure: the triangle is the energy stored; the rectangle is the energy supplied by the battery

alt: Displacement-time graph of the accelerating car (s = 0.75t²): the curve steepens, and the tangent at t = 4.0 s passes through (2.0 s, 0 m) and (6.0 s, 24.0 m), so its gradient, the velocity at that instant, is 6.0 m/s.
caption: Figure: the velocity at an instant is the gradient of the tangent

alt: An electron moving at 3.0 × 10⁷ m/s at right angles to a 2.0 mT field into the page: the magnetic force BQv is always perpendicular to the velocity, towards the centre, so the electron moves in a circle of radius mv/(BQ) = 8.5 cm at constant speed.
caption: Figure: a charged particle moves in a circle in a uniform magnetic field

alt: Charles's law: volume of a fixed mass of gas at constant pressure against Celsius temperature is a straight line; extrapolated backwards (dashed) it meets the temperature axis at about −273 °C, the estimate of absolute zero, where the volume would be zero.
caption: Figure: extrapolating V against θ to zero volume gives about −273 °C

alt: Before-and-after pictures: a 2.0 kg trolley at 3.0 m/s sticking to a stationary 1.0 kg trolley moves off at 2.0 m/s (momentum 6.0 kg m/s, kinetic energy 9.0 J to 6.0 J); a 0.40 kg ball at 5.0 m/s hitting a 0.60 kg ball elastically gives -1.0 and 4.0 m/s with total momentum 2.0 kg m/s unchanged.
caption: Figure: momentum is the same before and after; kinetic energy is lost only when the trolleys stick

alt: Conical pendulum, a 0.20 kg bob on a 0.80 m string at 30° to the vertical: radius 0.40 m; the vertical component of tension T cos 30° balances the weight 1.96 N (T = 2.27 N) and the horizontal component T sin 30° is the centripetal force, giving ω = 3.76 rad/s.
caption: Figure: forces on a conical pendulum bob

alt: Two force-time graphs for a 1200 kg car stopping from 15 m/s: a rigid car stops in 20 ms with a force of 900 kN, a crumple zone stops it in 90 ms with 200 kN; the areas are equal (18 000 N s) so a longer time means a much smaller force.
caption: Figure: same impulse, different stopping times (rigid car against crumple zone)

alt: Current-balance results for a 5.0 cm wire: the change in balance reading rises in proportion to the current (0.32 g at 1.0 A to 1.52 g at 5.0 A), a straight line through the origin of gradient 0.304 g per A, giving B = 0.0596 T.
caption: Figure: current balance, balance change against current (points from the lesson table)

alt: Current-time graph: a current falling steadily from 4.0 mA to zero in 10 s; the area under the line, a triangle of ½ × 4.0 × 10⁻³ A × 10 s, is the charge that flowed, 0.020 C.
caption: Figure: charge is the area under a current-time graph

alt: Corrected count rate against time for the short-lived gas source: an exponential fall from 40.0 per second, with equal fractions lost in equal times; the rate halves to 20 per second after about 56.6 s, the half-life.
caption: Figure: radioactive decay is exponential; the half-life is read from the curve

alt: Graph of ln R against t for the decay data: a straight line from 3.69 at t = 0 to 2.22 at 120 s, with gradient −0.01225 per second, so the decay constant is 0.0123 per second and the half-life 56.6 s.
caption: Figure: ln R against t is a straight line of gradient −λ

alt: Wavefronts from a source moving to the right: each is a circle centred where it was emitted, so they are bunched together ahead of the source (shorter wavelength, higher pitch) and spread out behind it; for the lesson's 900 Hz siren at 25 m/s the observer ahead hears 971 Hz and the one behind 838 Hz.
caption: Figure: the Doppler effect for a moving source (speed exaggerated in the drawing)

alt: Fringe pattern from Young's double slit (slit separation 0.50 mm, screen 1.80 m away, laser light of wavelength 600 nm): equally spaced bright fringes with centres 2.16 mm apart, found from x = λD/a, with dark fringes midway between them.
caption: Figure: the double-slit intensity pattern has equally spaced bright fringes of separation x = λD/a

alt: Gravitational potential of the Earth against distance from its centre: a −1/r curve starting at −6.25 × 10⁷ J/kg at the surface (6.37 × 10⁶ m), −3.13 × 10⁷ at twice that distance, and rising ever more gently towards zero at infinity.
caption: Figure: potential is negative everywhere and rises towards zero with distance

alt: Terminal p.d. against current for a battery pack: six points fall on a straight line sloping down; the intercept on the V axis, about 4.51 V, is the e.m.f., and the gradient, about −1.21 V per A, gives the internal resistance, about 1.2 ohms.
caption: Figure: V = E − Ir, so the intercept is the e.m.f. and the gradient is minus the internal resistance

alt: Energy against height for a 0.15 kg ball dropped from 20 m: EP falls in a straight line from 29.4 J to zero while EK rises by the same amount in free fall (total constant); with air resistance EK reaches only 23.2 J at the ground, the other 6.2 J being work done against drag.
caption: Figure: energy against height for a falling ball, with and without air resistance

alt: Graph of resistance against temperature with a false origin (the temperature axis starts at 20 °C): seven points lie on a straight line; the large gradient triangle between (25.0 °C, 13.20 Ω) and (75.0 °C, 15.61 Ω) gives a gradient of 0.0482 Ω per °C, and the intercept 12.0 Ω must be calculated, not read from the graph.
caption: Figure: choose points far apart on the line for the gradient; with a false origin calculate the intercept

alt: I-V graph of the 12 V vehicle lamp from the table: the curve through the origin bends towards the V axis, so resistance V/I rises from 1.61 Ω at 1.0 V to 3.80 Ω at 6.0 V and 5.71 Ω at 12.0 V; the dashed chord to the 12 V point has gradient 1/R.
caption: Figure: I-V characteristic of a filament lamp (points from the lesson table)

alt: Fleming's left-hand rule: the first finger gives the field direction (north to south), the second finger the conventional current and the thumb the motion or force, all three at right angles; with the field to the right and the current up the force is into the page (drawn up and to the right in this oblique sketch); reversing either the field or the current reverses the force.
caption: Figure: Fleming's left-hand rule for the motor effect (three mutually perpendicular directions)

alt: Flux linkage against time for a 500-turn coil: NΦ rises steadily from 0 to 2.0 × 10⁻² Wb in 0.2 s, stays constant until 0.4 s, then falls to zero by 0.6 s; the gradient (the e.m.f.) is 0.10 V, then zero, then −0.10 V.
caption: Figure: the induced e.m.f. is the gradient of the flux-linkage graph

alt: A rope pulls a scotch cart 25 m at 35° above the horizontal with a tension of 120 N: only the horizontal component 98.3 N does work, W = 120 × 25 × cos 35° = 2457 J, and the vertical component 68.8 N does none.
caption: Figure: only the component of the force along the displacement does work

alt: Force-displacement graph: the force rises steadily from 0 to 60 N over 0.30 m then stays at 60 N for a further 0.20 m; the work done is the area under the graph, a 9.0 J triangle plus a 12 J rectangle, 21 J in total.
caption: Figure: work done is the area under a force-displacement graph

alt: Graph of Earth's gravitational field strength against distance from its centre in Earth radii: it starts at 9.81 N/kg at the surface, falls to 2.45 at 2 radii and 0.613 at 4 radii, an inverse-square curve that approaches zero but never reaches it.
caption: Figure: g falls as 1/r² (points from the lesson table)

alt: Generator e.m.f. against the angle of the coil's normal from the field: a sine curve E = 113 sin θ with peak 113 V at 90° and 270° (coil plane parallel to the field) and zero at 0°, 180° and 360° (coil plane perpendicular to the field); 56.5 V at 30°.
caption: Figure: e.m.f. of the a.c. generator (200 turns, 0.012 m², 50 rev/s, 0.15 T) over one rotation

alt: Diffraction grating with 500 lines per mm (d = 2.00 µm) and 589 nm sodium light at normal incidence: maxima appear at 0° and on each side at 17.1° (first order), 36.1° (second) and 62.1° (third); the fourth order would need sin θ > 1, so seven maxima are seen.
caption: Figure: the seven orders from a 500 lines/mm grating (angles from d sin θ = nλ)

alt: Gravitational field lines: around a sphere they run straight inwards to the centre and spread out with distance, so the field weakens; near the ground over a small region they are parallel, vertical and equally spaced, a uniform field.
caption: Figure: gravitational field lines, radial (left) and nearly uniform near the surface (right)

alt: Heating curve for 0.10 kg of ice at −20 °C on a 500 W heater: ice warms for 8.4 s, melts at 0 °C for 67 s, water warms to 100 °C over 84 s and boils at 100 °C for 452 s; the flat sections are the energy mL and the boiling section is longest because Lv is about seven times Lf.
caption: Figure: heating curve of 0.10 kg of ice at 500 W (c ice 2100, c water 4200 J/kg/K, Lf 3.34 × 10⁵, Lv 2.26 × 10⁶ J/kg)

alt: Hydrogen energy-level diagram to scale: levels at −13.60, −3.40, −1.51, −0.85 and −0.54 eV closing up towards 0 eV; the fall from n = 3 to n = 2 emits 1.89 eV (658 nm, red), 4 to 2 emits 2.55 eV (488 nm, blue-green), and raising the electron from n = 1 to infinity takes 13.6 eV (91.4 nm).
caption: Figure: energy levels of hydrogen and three transitions from the worked examples

alt: Induced e.m.f. against time for the same coil: +0.10 V from 0 to 0.2 s while the flux linkage rises, zero from 0.2 to 0.4 s while it is constant, and −0.10 V from 0.4 to 0.6 s while it falls.
caption: Figure: e.m.f. against time for the flux-linkage graph above

alt: Path of the goalkeeper's kick (18 m/s at 35° above the horizontal): a parabola of range 31.0 m and maximum height 5.43 m, with a constant horizontal velocity component 14.7 m/s and a vertical component that is zero at the top and negative on the way down.
caption: Figure: a parabolic path; horizontal velocity stays constant while vertical velocity changes

alt: Force-time graph for the kicked ball: the force rises steadily to 600 N and falls to zero over 12 ms, a triangle whose area, ½ × 600 × 0.012 = 3.6 N s, is the impulse and the ball's change in momentum.
caption: Figure: impulse is the area under a force-time graph (kicked ball)

alt: Circuit for the Kirchhoff worked example: three branches between X (top) and Y (bottom), a 6.0 V battery with 2.0 ohms, a 4.0 V battery with 4.0 ohms, and a 6.0 ohm resistor; the currents are I1 = 0.818 A and I3 = 0.727 A, with I2 = −0.091 A, negative because current actually flows down through the 4.0 V battery.
caption: Figure: the three-branch circuit with the currents from the worked solution

alt: Velocity-time graph of the kombi: it accelerates uniformly from rest to 20 m/s in 8 s (gradient 2.5 m/s²), moves at 20 m/s for 30 s, then slows to rest in 12 s; the areas under the three sections are 80 m, 600 m and 120 m, a total displacement of 800 m.
caption: Figure: the area under the v-t graph is the displacement, 800 m

alt: Free-body diagram of a 5.0 m, 200 N ladder at 60° to rough ground against a smooth wall: the weight 200 N acts down at the centre, the wall pushes horizontally with 57.7 N, and at the foot the ground gives an upward reaction of 200 N and friction of 57.7 N towards the wall.
caption: Figure: the four forces on the ladder (arrow lengths drawn to one scale)

alt: A 50 N lamp hangs from two cables at 30° and 60° to the horizontal. The three forces, drawn tip to tail, form a closed right-angled triangle with the weight (50 N) as hypotenuse, giving tensions of 25.0 N and 43.3 N; the steeper cable carries more.
caption: Figure: the cable tensions from a closed triangle of forces

alt: Lenz's law: as a north pole is pushed into a coil, the induced current makes the near end of the coil a north pole, which repels the magnet; the work done against this repulsion is the energy that appears as electrical energy.
caption: Figure: the induced current opposes the approaching north pole

alt: Free-body diagram of a 70 kg person in a lift accelerating upwards at 1.5 m s⁻²: the contact force R = 792 N upwards is larger than the weight 687 N downwards, and the resultant of 105 N upwards equals ma.
caption: Figure: free-body diagram for the lift (arrow lengths drawn to scale)

alt: Light damping: a pendulum starting at 10.0 cm oscillates with the amplitude multiplied by 0.80 every cycle (10.0, 8.0, 6.4, 5.1, 4.1, 3.3 cm), a smooth exponential envelope, while the period stays almost constant; each cycle loses 36% of the energy.
caption: Figure: lightly damped oscillation with an exponential decay in amplitude

alt: Snapshot of a sound wave (amplitude 5.0 µm, wavelength 0.60 m): the displacement-distance graph is a sine curve, and the particles crowd into a compression at x = 0.300 m, where displacement changes from positive (right) to negative (left), and spread into rarefactions at 0 and 0.600 m.
caption: Figure: a longitudinal wave, particle positions above the matching displacement graph (points from the lesson table)

alt: Mains voltage against time: a sine wave of peak 325 V and period 20 ms (50 Hz) that swings between +325 V and −325 V; the dashed line at 230 V is the r.m.s. value, the steady d.c. voltage that would give the same heating power.
caption: Figure: 230 V r.m.s. mains has a peak of 325 V and a period of 20 ms

alt: Malus's law: transmitted intensity I/I₀ = cos²θ falls from 1.000 at 0° through 0.750 at 30°, 0.500 at 45° and 0.250 at 60° to zero at 90°, then rises again to 1 at 180° as the filter is turned.
caption: Figure: transmitted intensity through a polarising filter against angle (points from the lesson table)

alt: Mass spectrometer: neon ions at 4.0 × 10⁵ m/s enter a 0.50 T field and move in semicircles with r = mv/(BQ) proportional to mass; neon-20 has r = 0.166 m and neon-22 r = 0.183 m, so they land 3.3 cm apart.
caption: Figure: heavier isotopes follow larger semicircles in a mass spectrometer

alt: I-V graph of a metal wire at constant temperature: a straight line through the origin in both directions, so V/I is the same at every point and the wire is ohmic.
caption: Figure: an ohmic conductor at constant temperature (sketch)

alt: Uniform electric field between two parallel plates a distance d apart: equally spaced parallel field lines run from the positive plate to the negative plate, and the field strength is E = V/d.
caption: Figure: the field between parallel plates is uniform, E = V/d

alt: Maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons against frequency for a metal of work function 2.28 eV: a straight line with gradient h/e (about 4.1 × 10⁻¹⁵ V s), crossing the frequency axis at the threshold frequency 5.51 × 10¹⁴ Hz and the energy axis at −2.28 eV; no electrons are emitted below the threshold.
caption: Figure: Einstein's equation as a straight line: gradient h/e, intercepts f₀ and −Φ

alt: Stationary waves in a 0.33 m pipe with sound at 340 m/s: a pipe closed at one end has a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, giving 258 Hz (a quarter wavelength) then 773 Hz (three quarters of a wavelength); a pipe open at both ends has antinodes at both ends, giving 515 Hz for a half wavelength.
caption: Figure: the displacement pattern in closed and open pipes (L = 0.33 m)

alt: Force-extension graph for a wire stretched past its elastic limit: the line is straight up to the limit of proportionality, then curves in the plastic region; on unloading the line is parallel to the original straight part and meets the extension axis away from zero, leaving a permanent extension.
caption: Figure: unloading beyond the elastic limit leaves a permanent extension (sketch)

alt: Graph of electric potential against distance from a +12 nC point charge: a 1/r curve from 1080 V at 0.10 m to 180 V at 0.60 m; the tangent at 0.20 m has gradient about -2698 V/m, so the field strength there is about 2698 V/m (N/C).
caption: Figure: the field strength is minus the gradient of the tangent to the V-r curve

alt: Potential divider: a 9.0 V battery across a 4.7 kΩ resistor in series with a 2.2 kΩ resistor; the output taken across the 2.2 kΩ resistor is 9.0 × 2.2/6.9 = 2.87 V, and the other resistor has 6.13 V across it.
caption: Figure: the supply p.d. divides in proportion to resistance; the output is taken across R₂

alt: Potentiometer circuit: a driver cell with rheostat across the 100.0 cm wire AB gives 2.00 V (0.0200 V per cm); a test cell in series with a galvanometer and a jockey balances at 72.5 cm so no current flows in the test cell and its e.m.f. is 0.0200 × 72.5 = 1.45 V.
caption: Figure: a potentiometer balanced at 72.5 cm, giving E = 1.45 V

alt: Driving force against speed for a 1000 kg car with maximum power 60 kW: the curve F = P/v gives 3000 N at 20 m/s, where the resistive force is 1200 N, leaving a resultant of 1800 N (a = 1.8 m/s²); at 30 m/s the force is 2000 N, equal to the resistive force, so 30 m/s is the top speed.
caption: Figure: full-power driving force falls as speed rises until it equals the resistive force

alt: Three output graphs for a 50 Hz supply with peak 17.0 V: (a) half-wave rectification gives one hump every 20 ms with gaps of zero; (b) full-wave gives a hump every 10 ms with no gaps; (c) a 220 µF smoothing capacitor across a 500 Ω load holds the output near 17 V with a ripple of about 1.3 V.
caption: Figure: half-wave, full-wave and smoothed full-wave output (peak 17.0 V, 50 Hz)

alt: Resonance curves for a system with natural frequency 2.0 Hz: with light damping the amplitude ratio peaks at 12.57 at 2.0 Hz; with heavier damping the peak is much lower (about 2.1) and broader and sits slightly below 2.0 Hz; far from resonance both curves agree, falling towards zero above 3 Hz.
caption: Figure: more damping lowers and broadens the resonance peak (points from the lesson table)

alt: Ripple-tank wavefronts meeting a barrier: through a gap of 10 wavelengths the waves continue almost straight with only slight bending at the edges and a clear shadow; through a gap of one wavelength they spread out as nearly semicircular wavefronts; the wavelength is the same before and after the gap.
caption: Figure: diffraction is strongest when the gap is about one wavelength

alt: Series-parallel circuit on a 12 V supply: a 2.0 Ω resistor in series with 6.0 Ω and 12 Ω in parallel (4.0 Ω together); the supply current is 2.0 A, 4.0 V across the 2.0 Ω and 8.0 V across the pair, which carry 1.33 A and 0.667 A.
caption: Figure: the worked series-parallel network with currents and p.d.s

alt: Acceleration against displacement for the spring oscillator: a straight line through the origin from +3.2 m/s² at x = −8.0 cm to −3.2 m/s² at x = +8.0 cm, with gradient −ω² = −40 per s², which is the defining test for simple harmonic motion.
caption: Figure: a = −ω²x is a straight line of negative gradient through the origin

alt: Energy against displacement for a 0.40 kg s.h.m. oscillator (ω = 5.0 rad/s, amplitude 0.10 m): the total energy 0.050 J is constant; potential energy is an upward parabola from zero at x = 0, kinetic energy an inverted parabola reaching 0.050 J at x = 0, and they are equal (0.025 J) at x = ±0.071 m.
caption: Figure: kinetic and potential energy trade places while the total stays constant

alt: Graphs of s.h.m. for a 0.50 kg mass on a 20 N/m spring (amplitude 8.0 cm, period 0.993 s) against time in periods: displacement is a sine curve, velocity a cosine curve a quarter cycle ahead (maximum 0.51 m/s), and acceleration an inverted sine curve in antiphase with displacement (maximum 3.20 m/s²).
caption: Figure: displacement, velocity and acceleration in s.h.m. over one period

alt: I-V graph of a silicon diode: no current in reverse bias or below about 0.6 V forward, then the current rises very steeply (1.2 mA at 0.60 V, 18 mA at 0.70 V, 55 mA at 0.75 V), so its resistance falls from 500 Ω to 38.9 Ω.
caption: Figure: I-V characteristic of a silicon diode (points from the lesson table)

alt: Free-body diagram of a trolley on a smooth 25° ramp: weight mg straight down and the normal force R = mg cos 25° perpendicular to the slope; the unbalanced component mg sin 25° along the slope gives a = g sin 25° = 4.15 m s⁻².
caption: Figure: forces on a trolley on a smooth 25° incline

alt: A spanner 0.30 m long is pulled at its end by a 150 N force at 60° to the spanner. The perpendicular distance from the nut to the line of action of the force is 0.30 sin 60° = 0.260 m, so the moment is 150 × 0.260 = 39.0 N m, less than the 45 N m from a force at 90°.
caption: Figure: only the perpendicular distance to the line of action counts

alt: Force-extension graph for the catapult spring (k = 250 N/m): the straight line reaches 20 N at an extension of 0.080 m, and the area under it, ½ × 20 × 0.080 = 0.80 J, is the elastic potential energy stored.
caption: Figure: elastic energy is the area under the force-extension graph (k = 250 N/m, x = 8.0 cm)

alt: Force-extension graph for the spring: the first six points (0 to 5.0 N, extension up to 12.5 cm) lie on a straight line through the origin of gradient 40 N/m, so Hooke's law holds; the 6.0 N point at 16.2 cm lies below that line, past the limit of proportionality.
caption: Figure: Hooke's law holds up to the limit of proportionality, where the graph bends

alt: Magnetic field of a long straight wire carrying current out of the page: concentric circles around the wire, drawn anticlockwise, with spacing that grows with distance because the field weakens.
caption: Figure: field lines of a long straight wire (current out of the page)

alt: Stress-strain graph for a ductile metal such as copper or mild steel: a straight line from the origin whose gradient is the Young modulus up to the limit of proportionality, then a yield point where strain rises with little extra stress, a maximum at the ultimate tensile stress, and a breaking point below it as the wire necks.
caption: Figure: stress-strain curve of a ductile metal (shape only; no scale)

alt: A string 0.80 m long fixed at both ends, with waves travelling at 120 m/s: the first three stationary-wave patterns have 1, 2 and 3 loops, with nodes at the ends and between loops, wavelengths 1.60 m, 0.80 m and 0.53 m, and frequencies 75 Hz, 150 Hz and 225 Hz.
caption: Figure: the first three harmonics of a string fixed at both ends

alt: Velocity-time graph for an 80 kg skydiver with drag 0.25v²: it starts with gradient 9.81 m/s², curves over as drag grows and levels off at the terminal velocity 56.0 m/s (18.9 m/s at 2 s, 49.6 m/s at 8 s) where drag equals weight.
caption: Figure: velocity-time graph of a skydiver reaching terminal velocity

alt: Calibration curve for an NTC thermistor (illustrative values): resistance plotted against temperature measured with a standard thermometer falls in a curve from about 29 kΩ at 0 °C to under 1 kΩ at 100 °C; a later resistance reading is converted to a temperature by reading across to the curve and down to the axis.
caption: Figure: a calibration curve converts a sensor reading into a value of the quantity

alt: Velocity-time graph for a ball thrown up at 12 m/s: one straight line of gradient −9.81 m/s² crossing zero at the top of the flight (t = 1.22 s); the triangle above the axis is +7.3 m (maximum height) and the equal triangle below is −7.3 m, so the net displacement is zero.
caption: Figure: one straight line for the whole flight; areas above and below the axis cancel

alt: Step-down transformer on a laminated soft-iron core: 1150 primary turns on 230 V and 60 secondary turns give 12 V to a 24 W lamp; the secondary current is 2.0 A and the primary current only 0.104 A, so Vs/Vp = Ns/Np = Ip/Is.
caption: Figure: an ideal step-down transformer (1150 turns to 60 turns) lighting a 12 V, 24 W lamp

alt: Vector triangle for two tractor pulls of 40 kN and 30 kN with 60° between the chains: placed tip to tail the resultant closes the triangle, R = 60.8 kN at 25.3° to the 40 kN chain (angle opposite R is 120°).
caption: Figure: adding two forces tip to tail (scale drawing, 1 kN = 4.2 px)

alt: Forces on a 0.20 kg mass in a vertical circle of radius 0.60 m: at the top (3.0 m/s) tension 1.04 N and weight 1.96 N both point to the centre; at the bottom (5.0 m/s) tension 10.3 N upwards exceeds the weight, so the string is most likely to break at the bottom.
caption: Figure: tension at the top and bottom of a vertical circle

alt: Snapshot of a wave on a rope (displacement against distance): one full sine curve of amplitude 3.0 cm repeating every 0.80 m, so the wavelength is read from the horizontal axis as the distance between adjacent crests.
caption: Figure: displacement-distance graph; the horizontal gap between crests is the wavelength

alt: Displacement-time graph for one point on the wave: the same sine shape, but now the horizontal gap between crests is the period T, the time for one oscillation, and the frequency is 1/T.
caption: Figure: displacement-time graph; the horizontal gap between crests is the period

alt: Magnetic flux density near a long wire carrying 12 A against 1/r: the points (r = 1, 2, 4 and 8 cm, B = 240, 120, 60 and 30 microtesla) lie on a straight line through the origin of gradient 240 µT cm, showing B is inversely proportional to the distance.
caption: Figure: B against 1/r is a straight line through the origin
